The fallout from the Middle East war will figure prominently in the discussions during this year's Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) meet, as the Philippines seeks a joint response to the crisis and the implementation of a power grid deal under its chairmanship of the regional bloc.

Foreign Affairs Assistant Secretary Dominic Xavier Imperial said the ASEAN leaders’ statement on the response to the Middle East crisis is one of the three outcome documents that the Philippines aims to endorse for the consideration of the regional bloc's leaders.

"The leaders’ statement outlines ASEAN’s collective response to the crisis while building the foundation for stronger coordination in future emergencies," Imperial said at a press briefing on Wednesday here.

Even if the US, whose attack against Iran had sparked the latest Middle East conflict, is an ASEAN partner, no impediment is expected to affect the issuance of the joint statement.

"We’re actually very confident about the declaration on how ASEAN will respond to the Middle East crisis. We do not see any impediment, in fact, we are very encouraged by the commitment of all the ASEAN member states," Imperial said.

"The main purpose rally here is for all the member states ASEAN to be able to come up with measures that will help us respond not only to the current situation now also to other future crisis," he added.

Imperial said upholding ASEAN centrality, which prods the bloc to be at the center of every discussion on vital issues, is also a priority of the Philippines as chairman and the principle is being seen in the crafting of the joint statement.

Asked if the ASEAN would issue an appeal for the US and other parties to put an end to the war, Imperial replied: "The document is being negotiated, so, I don’t want to preempt it but what I can share with you right now is there will definitely be a reference to that."

The conflict, which erupted last Feb. 28 after US and Israel mounted air strikes against Iran, is widely seen to disrupt international supply chains and pose serious risks to regional and global security. The US and Iran agreed to observe a ceasefire last month.

Aside from the joint response to the Middle East war, the other outcome documents being pushed by the Philippines are the Cebu Protocol, which seeks to amend the ASEAN charter to fully integrate its newest member Timor Leste into the bloc; and the ASEAN leaders’ declaration on maritime cooperation.

In the same press briefing, Trade Undersecretary Allan Gepty said the implementation of the memorandum of understanding (MOU) on ASEAN power grid is among the priority economic deliverables in the 48th ASEAN Summit. He noted that the MOU is envisioned to allow cross-border trade of electricity.

"This basically will lay down the framework both legal, technical and even the policy aspect of this to ensure and also pave the way for the connectivity in cross-border trade of electricity through submarine power cable," Gepty said.

"With the current situation right now in the Middle East and the adverse effects to the region and to the global economy, it emphasizes the need for more integration and more cooperation in the region."

According to Gepty, the adverse effect of the Middle East crisis is a reminder that the world is integrated and interconnected and that no country can navigate external shocks or disruptions alone.

"It is timely that of the many priority economic deliverables of the Philippines under its chairship right now, they are very strategic and very helpful in providing medium-term and long-term solutions to the adverse effects of the crisis," the trade official said.

The other economic deliverables under the Philippines' leadership of ASEAN are promoting regenerative and resilient agriculture system for better and sustainable farming practices; promoting foreign investments in high-growth and green sectors to fast track green transition; providing a set of rules to promote digital trade; promoting innovation and creative industries; and the completion of important trade agreement such as the ASEAN-Canada Free Trade Agreement. | via @alexisbromero

During Exercise Balikatan 2026 in the Philippines, the U.S. military used a target vessel converted from a small remote-controlled high-speed boat to simulate a PLA ZBD-05 amphibious assault vehicle.

The target craft is about 9 meters long, roughly 90% the size of the actual ZBD-05, and capable of speeds exceeding 30 knots (around 56 km/h), allowing it to realistically replicate a high-speed amphibious assault target during live-fire training.
